title: Draupadi's question
hook: a messenger walks to Draupadi's door and comes back carrying a question: whom did you lose first?
carry: whom did you lose first, yourself or me

segments.voice: Yesterday the last stakes of the dice game fell: the twins, Arjuna, Bhima, Yudhishthira himself, and then Draupadi. This week ran from Duryodhana's stumble in Maya's hall to the last stake in the dice hall. Your line was name it plainly, the way he did. Which moment from the whole week stays with you? Day seven hundred seventy.

The game is over, and Duryodhana wants Draupadi brought into the hall. First he tells Vidura to fetch her. Vidura refuses flatly. In the telling, he says she can't have become anyone's slave, because Yudhishthira staked her after he'd already lost himself. Hold on to that. It's the thread of everything that follows. Duryodhana turns instead to an usher, a servant whose job is carrying messages, and sends him to the women's rooms. Today, a messenger walks to Draupadi's door, and walks back carrying a question.
screen: `VIDURA REFUSES TO FETCH HER.` → `HE LOST HIMSELF FIRST.` → `A MESSENGER AT HER DOOR.`

segments.voice: The usher tells Draupadi what has happened: Yudhishthira, carried away by the game, has lost her to Duryodhana, and she must come. Draupadi doesn't come. She asks him to go back and put one thing to the gambler in the hall: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? It's a precise question. If he lost himself first, he was no longer free when he staked her, and perhaps had nothing left to stake. If he staked her first, the answer is different. She isn't pleading. She's asking for the facts the whole claim rests on. The usher carries it back and asks it in the hall. And Yudhishthira says nothing. The telling says he sits as if he's lost his senses, and answers not a word, good or bad. Duryodhana tells the usher: let her come here and ask it herself. The usher goes back, uneasy, and Draupadi sends him again. This time her question isn't only for Yudhishthira. Ask the assembly, she says, what is right for me to do, and I'll do it. Watch how the question grows. First it was for one man. Now it's for a whole hall of kings and elders. The usher, caught between a furious prince and a woman who won't be moved, hesitates to go a third time. So Duryodhana sends his brother Duhshasana instead. The messenger stage is over. And the question, still unanswered, is about to walk into the hall in person.
screen: `THE USHER: YOU'VE BEEN LOST.` · `WHOM DID YOU LOSE FIRST?` · `YUDHISHTHIRA SAYS NOTHING.` · `ASK THE WHOLE ASSEMBLY.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION GROWS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow, and the hands rest open. Bring to mind a question you've been wanting to ask but haven't: about a decision made for you, or something that didn't add up. Don't answer it. Just let it take shape, as plainly as Draupadi's did. Who decided? On what grounds? Hold your question gently, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer. If not, let it sit with you in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's question. Sent back with a messenger: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? Then sent to the whole hall.
Your line: whom did you lose first, yourself or me. Today, when a decision lands on you, ask one plain question about how it was made. Day seven hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Draupadi's question is retold in homes, dance and theater, and it's discussed by readers and commentators as a question about dharma and law that the epic leaves open.

fork.setup: you're the usher. Yudhishthira won't answer Draupadi's question, and Duryodhana says: let her come and ask it herself. what do you do?
options: go back and tell her what he said.
fork.reveal: he goes back to her, and Draupadi sends him again, this time to ask the whole assembly what is right.

original.note: Sanskrit praśna: a question; also the name of the Prashna Upanishad, built on questions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman refusing to come.
what it means: a woman asking for the facts the whole claim rests on: whom did you lose first?
what a scholar hears: the question turns on whether a man who has lost himself still owns anything to stake, a point of law the hall will argue over.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duryodhana sends Vidura, who refuses; the usher Pratikamin sent to Draupadi; her question whether Yudhishthira lost himself first; Yudhishthira's silence; the second message to the assembly; Duhshasana sent)

notes: Week end (day 770): the review looks back on the week. The week (764–770) runs from Duryodhana in Maya's hall to the last stake.
All paraphrase. Confirm Vidura's refusal and his reason (she was staked after Yudhishthira lost himself).
Confirm the usher (Pratikamin) and Draupadi's question 'whom did you lose first, yourself or me', and Yudhishthira's silence 'like one deprived of sense, answering not a word, good or bad'.
Confirm Draupadi's second message asking the assembly what is right; the usher's hesitation is kept general (Ganguli gives fear of Bhima or of Draupadi's anger as a reason).
The usher is unnamed in the voice to keep the scene simple; a Keeper may want 'Pratikamin' named.
